author: Coffee With Sumeet Jain
keywords: first inr line of credit nepal
china belt and road nepal counter
short_description:
MODI ने Balen Shah की तबीयत से हेकड़ी निकाली, औकात दिखा कर 25 घंटों में वापस भेज दिया | CWSJ-3906

Why did Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah cut his maiden state visit to New Delhi from three days down to a lightning-fast 25 hours? On the surface, mainstream headlines called it a routine diplomatic reset. In reality, Prime Minister Narendra Modi just executed one of South Asia's sharpest financial and maritime masterstrokes—displacing the US Dollar in neighborhood lending while physically neutralizing China's Belt and Road rail leverage in the Himalayas.

In this deep-dive investigative episode of Coffee With Sumeet Jain, we connect the hidden dots behind the ₹15,000 crore India-Nepal development package signed on November 23, 2026. Following devastating August 2026 floods, Kathmandu arrived in New Delhi seeking $2 billion in aid and access to private Adani-operated ports at Mundra and Dhamra. Instead, India structured a ₹3,500 crore grant alongside India's first-ever ₹11,500 crore Indian Rupee-denominated Line of Credit strictly tied to energy projects—locking Nepal's hydropower sector into Indian currency, Indian builders, and India's 10,000 MW power trade grid while blocking Chinese contractors.

We also uncover why New Delhi declined Mundra and Dhamra ports and instead granted Nepal third-country transit access through government-operated Deendayal Port at Kandla in Gujarat and Paradip Port in Odisha, keeping customs and strategic oversight firmly under Indian control. From Mayor Balen Shah's 2023 Greater Nepal map controversy to his total silence on border disputes in Delhi, the Saryu-Kamala Express linking Ayodhya and Janakpur, and the unanswered mystery of demonetized 2016 Indian currency notes still locked in Kathmandu's vaults, here is the full unfiltered story and what it means for India's economy. Subscribe for daily geopolitical and economic intelligence.

title: INDIA ENTERED Stage 2 of Homi Bhabha's Plan | Plutonium-239, Liquid Sodium, Thorium Blanket, PFBR
author: Best of Tarun Bindlish
keywords: homi bhabha three stage nuclear programme
short_description:
▶ Full Episode:

Subscribe to Best of Tarun Bindlish:

Full episodes on the Main Channel:

India has only about 2% of the world's uranium but roughly a quarter of its thorium, and Homi Bhabha built a 100-year nuclear plan around that one fact. Abhijit Chavda explains Bhabha's three-stage programme: natural uranium in heavy water reactors, then plutonium in fast breeder reactors, and finally thorium for energy that could last centuries. He explains why the world's big nuclear powers never tried it, and why India had no choice.

Stage two has now gone live at Kalpakkam. A 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor reached a self-sustaining chain reaction, and it makes more fuel than it burns. Abhijit compares it with Russia's breeders and China's 2 MW molten-salt reactor, and explains the 20–22-year "doubling time" that decides how fast India can reach stage three. He then traces the sanctions after 1974 that put Tarapur's fuel supply at risk, the 2008 India–US nuclear deal, and the supplier-liability clause that kept Westinghouse and GE away. The conversation ends on why energy is now at the centre of geopolitics, and how AI data centres are creating a new demand for always-on power.


About the Guest — Abhijit Chavda
Abhijit Chavda is a geopolitical analyst, author and podcaster who works on India's strategic affairs, history and civilisation. On his own YouTube channel he explains defence, energy and global power politics from an Indian point of view.

author: PGurus

You close WhatsApp Web and walk away. Could the next person at that computer still see your chats?

India’s cybercrime coordination centre, I4C, has warned that closing a browser tab can leave a WhatsApp Web session active. On a shared computer, that could expose private conversations or let someone send messages in your name. PGurus coverage of the I4C advisory

Sree Iyer explains what the warning means for anyone who uses WhatsApp at work or on a shared device. Sign out when you finish. If you’ve already left the computer, open Linked Devices in WhatsApp on your phone, select the computer and tap Log out. WhatsApp’s official unlinking guide
